[[File:平安宮 中和院位置.png|thumb|250px|right|{{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|qid=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō}} {{ill|Heian Palace|ar|قصر هييان|ca|Palau Heian|cs|Palác Heian|de|Heian-Palast|es|Palacio Heian|fa|قصر هی‌آن|fi|Heian-palatsi|fr|Palais Heian|hu|Heian-palota|id|Istana Heian|ja|大内裏|jv|Istana Heian|ko|헤이안궁|mad|Istana Heian|ms|Istana Heian|pt|Palácio Heian|ru|Дворец Хэйан|sl|Palača Heian|sv|Heianpalatset|ta|ஹெயன் அரண்மனை|th|พระราชวังหลวงเฮอัง|tr|Heian Sarayı|vi|Cung điện Heian|zh|平安宮|qid=Q304501|lt=Heian Palace}}, showing the location of Chūkain (中和院)]]
'''Chūkain''' (中和院/中院), also known as '''Nakain''' (中院), was a ceremonial hall located within the {{ill|Heian Palace|ar|قصر هييان|ca|Palau Heian|cs|Palác Heian|de|Heian-Palast|es|Palacio Heian|fa|قصر هی‌آن|fi|Heian-palatsi|fr|Palais Heian|hu|Heian-palota|id|Istana Heian|ja|大内裏|jv|Istana Heian|ko|헤이안궁|mad|Istana Heian|ms|Istana Heian|pt|Palácio Heian|ru|Дворец Хэйан|sl|Palača Heian|sv|Heianpalatset|ta|ஹெயன் அரண்மனை|th|พระราชวังหลวงเฮอัง|tr|Heian Sarayı|vi|Cung điện Heian|zh|平安宮|qid=Q304501}} (Daidairi) in {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|qid=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō}}. The site corresponds approximately to the current vicinity of Senbon Street and Shimodachiuri Street in {{ill|Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto|en|Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto|qid=Q1321824|lt=Kamigyō-ku}}, Kyoto.
== Overview ==
Chūkain was situated in the southwestern section of the {{ill|Inner Palace|ja|内裏外郭|qid=Q140447337}} within the Heian Palace. It was the site for the Emperor's personal participation in rituals such as the {{ill|Niiname-no-Matsuri|en|Niiname-no-Matsuri|qid=Q11501518|lt=Niinamesai}} (Harvest Festival, held annually in November) and the {{ill|Jinkonjiki|ja|神今食|qid=Q55535655}} (divine meals held in June and December). Constructed during the founding of the palace, it is referred to in historical records as "Chūkain," "Nakain," "Kamimiso-in," and "Saien."
The compound was enclosed by earthen walls and contained the '''Shinkaden''' (神嘉殿) as its main hall, along with the East and West Halls (東舎・西舎) and the North Hall (北殿). Corridors connected the Shinkaden to the other structures. The central area of the Shinkaden was partitioned to create a sacred space for rituals, where the Emperor symbolically shared food with {{ill|Amaterasu|en|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami}}. A similar ritual is still conducted at the {{ill|Tokyo Imperial Palace|ar|قصر طوكيو الإمبراطوري|arz|قصر طوكيو الامبراطورى|ca|Palau Imperial de Tòquio|cs|Kókjo|de|Kaiserpalast Tokio|el|Αυτοκρατορικό Παλάτι του Τόκιο|es|Kōkyo|eu|Tokioko Jauregi Inperiala|fa|کاخ امپراتوری توکیو|fi|Tokion keisarillinen palatsi|fr|Palais impérial de Tokyo|he|הארמון הקיסרי של טוקיו|hr|Carska palača u Tokiju|id|Istana Kekaisaran Tokyo|it|Palazzo imperiale di Tokyo|ja|皇居|ka|იმპერატორის სასახლე (ტოკიო)|ko|고쿄|la|Palatium Imperiale Tokiense|lt|Tokijo imperatoriškieji rūmai|min|Istano Kakaisaran Tokyo|mn|Токиогийн эзэн хааны ордон|ms|Istana Maharaja Tokyo|nl|Kokyo|no|Keiserpalasset i Tokyo|pl|Cesarski kompleks pałacowy w Tokio|pt|Palácio Imperial de Tóquio|ru|Императорский дворец в Токио|simple|Tokyo Imperial Palace|sl|Tokijska cesarska palača|su|Kokyo|sv|Kejsarpalatset i Tokyo|ta|டோக்கியோ அரண்மனை|th|พระราชวังหลวงโตเกียว|tr|Tokyo İmparatorluk Sarayı|uk|Токійський Імператорський палац|ur|جاپانی شاہی محل|vi|Hoàng cung Tokyo|wuu|东京皇居|zh|皇居|zh_min_nan|Hông-ku|zh_yue|皇居|qid=Q500681|lt=Kōkyū}} in Tokyo within the modern {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ar|معابد القصر الثلاثة|es|Santuarios de los Tres Palacios|fr|Trois Sanctuaires du Palais|id|Tiga Tempat Suci Istana|ja|宮中三殿|pt|Três Santuários do Palácio|zh|宮中三殿|qid=Q7797685|lt=Three Palace Sanctuaries}}, which includes a Shinkaden.
Chūkain was the first permanent ritual space to be separated from the emperor’s residential quarters, a significant development from earlier practices at {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|cs|Nagaoka-kjó|de|Nagaoka-kyō|es|Nagaoka-kyō|et|Nagaoka-kyō|eu|Nagaoka-kyo|fa|ناگائوکا-کیو|fi|Nagaoka-kyō|fr|Nagaoka-kyō|gl|Nagaoka-kyō|hy|Նագաոկակյո|id|Nagaoka-kyō|it|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京|ko|나가오카쿄|ms|Nagaoka-kyō|my|နဂအိုခခယော|nl|Nagaoka-kyo|pl|Nagaoka-kyō|pt|Nagaoka-kyō|ru|Нагаокакё (столица)|simple|Nagaoka-kyō|tr|Nagaoka-kyō|zh|長岡京|qid=Q1052803|lt=Nagaoka-kyō}}. Its central location within the Heian Palace reflects Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|en|Emperor Kanmu|qid=Q314846|lt=Kanmu}}'s vision of a ceremonial layout linking ancestral deities, the Emperor’s residence, and the symbolic presence of a retired emperor.<ref name="Hashimoto">Hashimoto Yoshinori, "The Structure of the Heian Palace," *Visiting the Heian Palace Ruins*, Kyoto Sōbunsya, 2011.</ref>
== History ==
The first documented reference to Nakain appears in {{ill|Nihon Kōki|en|Nihon Kōki|qid=Q1077029|lt=Nihon Kōki}} in 804, noting the collapse of its western tower. This suggests it existed during the initial construction of the Heian Palace. Some scholars propose that the "Chū" in the name signifies its central location, while others link it to the "Nakatomi" clan, known for its Shinto rituals.
Records such as {{ill|Ruijū Kokushi|en|Ruijū Kokushi|qid=Q1038639|lt=Ruiju Kokushi}} from 831 also use the name "Chūkain," but some scholars argue that the name became standardized after the Great Fire of 960 and the subsequent era of {{ill|Ōwa|en|Ōwa|qid=Q1324768|lt=Ōwa}}. alternate_name such as "Kamimiso-in" (神今食院) and "Saien" (斎院) appear in documents like the {{ill|Jōgan Gishiki|ja|貞観儀式|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11634544}} and {{ill|Seikyūki|ja|西宮記|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11627667}}.
In 1058, a major fire destroyed the 11 Imperial Palace and Chūkain, marking the first destruction of the Shinkaden since the capital's relocation to Heian-kyō. Subsequent fires in 1112 and 1163 also affected the site.<ref name="Hashimoto" />
Archaeological excavations conducted in the late 20th century revealed distinct stratigraphy and scattered tiles, confirming the location of ceremonial structures. The uncovered dimensions of the Shinkaden and associated findings such as volcanic tuff foundations highlight the site's architectural significance as a ritual center.<ref name="Hashimoto" />
== Structure ==
[[File:平安宮中和院跡出土 軒丸瓦.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Green-glazed roof tile from Chūkain}}{{small|Exhibited at the {{ill|Kyoto City Archaeological Museum|en|Kyoto City Archaeological Museum|qid=Q11375124|lt=Kyoto City Archaeological Museum}}.}}]]
Chūkain's central structure, the '''Shinkaden''', was surrounded by four enclosed walls and connected to auxiliary buildings via corridors. The Shinkaden was an east-west-oriented building with a layout of seven bays in width and two in depth, surrounded by covered galleries. The interior was divided into three sections, with the central area serving as the sacred space (神殿), the western section for the Emperor's seat, and the eastern section for attendants.
The East and West Halls, oriented north-south, were four bays in width and two in depth, with adjacent galleries. The North Hall, oriented east-west, was seven bays in width and two in depth, also featuring galleries.<ref name="Hashimoto" />
Excavations of the Shinkaden reveal it measured approximately 40 meters east-to-west and was built on a foundation of dressed volcanic tuff. The structure’s lack of extensive roofing tiles indicates its primary use as a ceremonial site. According to legend, the current {{ill|Isonokami Jingū|en|Isonokami Shrine|qid=Q708859|lt=Isonokami Shrine}} worship hall was relocated from the Shinkaden in 1081, although architectural evidence dates it to the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}.<ref>Miyazawa Satoshi, "Isonokami Shrine," *World Encyclopedia*, Heibonsha.</ref>
